source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) The double-edged sword of recombination in breakthrough innovation, SMJ 36(10)
finding: Two rival theories of creativity are tested at once. Tension view: distant and diverse recombination makes breakthroughs. Foundational view: deep local search finds anomalies and makes breakthroughs. The paper splits breakthrough into cognitive novelty and economic value. Both views turn out partly right, one for each outcome.
numbers: Hypotheses H1a/H1b (recombination -> citations), H2 (novelty -> citations), H3a/H3b (recombination -> novelty), tested as a mediation model (paths A, B, C).
quote: patents that originate new topics are more likely to be associated with local search, while economic value is the product of broader recombinations
limits: One technology domain (fullerenes and nanotubes). Patents only.
agent_relevance: Novelty and value need different search modes. A scaffold that wants new ideas should search near the problem in depth; one that wants useful ideas should also draw widely.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) data and sample
finding: Sample is all US fullerene and nanotube patents granted through 2008. Patents in one family were merged. Regressions use patents granted 1991-2005.
numbers: 2,826 patents; 2,384 patent families; 2,276 observations in the regressions; year fixed effects; 5-year forward citations from grant date.
limits: Fullerenes are a general purpose technology, so results may differ in narrow fields. Unpatented ideas are missing.
agent_relevance: Small single-domain sample: treat the effect directions as hypotheses, not as universal laws.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) topic-modeling measure of novelty
finding: Novelty is measured by LDA topic modelling on patent abstracts. A patent is topic-originating if it has at least 20% weight in a topic and falls in the first 12 months after that topic appears. Experts labelled the topics and picked the 0.20 threshold.
numbers: 100 topics; 3 expert coders; inter-coder reliability 0.78; 22 topics needed joint resolution; 25 topics judged too general; 189 topic-originating patents (mean 1.89 per topic, median 1); thresholds 0.15 and 0.25 gave qualitatively similar results; correlation of topics with USPTO classes 0.22.
limits: Sensitive to corpus choice, topic count (set to 100) and threshold. Counts only ideas that were patented.
agent_relevance: A text-based, code-run novelty test (new vocabulary arriving in a corpus) fits our rule that novelty is judged by running, not by opinion (G8).

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) distant and diverse recombination measures
finding: Distant recombination is technological distance between the classes a patent cites. Diverse recombination is the Hall-Jaffe-Trajtenberg originality index (one minus the sum of squared shares of cited patent classes), bias-corrected following Hall (2002). Controls come from Fleming (2001): time-discounted familiarity of components and combinations.
numbers: Originality set to 0 for patents with no prior art, with a dummy control.
limits: Class-based distance is a coarse proxy for how far apart ideas really are.
agent_relevance: Distance can be a code-computed number (embedding or class distance) that the scheduler uses to choose near or far search.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) Path C: recombination to citations (replication of prior work)
finding: Distant and diverse recombination raised citations, in the direction of earlier studies, but only technological distance was significant in the count model. For top-5% breakthroughs neither was significant.
numbers: Table 2 (generalized SEM, N=2276): distance 0.211 (SE 0.093, p<0.05); diversity 0.065 (SE 0.101, ns). Table 3 (top 5% outcome): distance and diversity not significant.
limits: Authors say the weaker result in Table 3 is likely due to lower variance in a binary outcome. Different field and period from earlier studies.
agent_relevance: Wide combination helps usefulness or reach; the effect is modest and not always significant.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) Path B: novelty to value
finding: Topic-originating patents get more citations and are more likely to be top-5% cited, but most novel patents are not highly cited and few highly cited ones are novel.
numbers: Citation coefficient 0.330 (SE 0.094, p<0.01), about 1.4 times the citations. Odds of top-5% breakthrough x1.7 (coef 0.538, SE 0.188). Probability 0.072 vs 0.024. Marginal effect 0.031. Mean 5-yr citations 22.17 for novel vs 12.77 for others. Only 20 of 189 novel patents are in the top 5% (109 top-cited patents in total); fewer than 1% of the sample is both.
limits: Citations measure usefulness, not novelty or true economic value. Selection on grant and citation.
agent_relevance: Novelty raises the chance of a hit but most novel ideas are not hits. Selecting promising novelty is the hard step.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) Path A: recombination to novelty (the surprise)
finding: Distant and diverse recombination made novel topic-originating patents LESS likely. Novelty came from local, deep search. The direct citation benefit of wide recombination was cancelled by this negative route, so the total effect of distance on citations was near zero.
numbers: Table 2 path A (row order read from a text extraction of the PDF table, so assignment of the two rows is likely but not certain): distance -0.391 (SE 0.184, p<0.05), diversity -0.486 (SE 0.167, p<0.01). Indirect effects via novelty: distance -0.129 (p<0.05), diversity -0.158 (p<0.01). Total effect on citations: distance 0.082 (SE 0.119, ns), diversity -0.093 (SE 0.118, ns). Table 3 indirect effects -0.209 and -0.257. Inventor experience was the only control that raised novelty.
limits: Observational. Authors note simultaneous choice of novelty and value (endogeneity). GSEM with 1000 bootstrap repetitions.
agent_relevance: Do not assume far analogies are what create new ideas. Keep a deep-in-domain mode (find anomalies and failing cases) alongside a far-search mode; do not use far search as the default novelty engine.

source: Kaplan & Vakili (2015) theoretical sources: tension vs foundational creativity
finding: Tension view (Weisberg 1999; Hargadon & Sutton 1997; Ahuja & Lampert 2001): deep knowledge causes lock-in, so wide recombination is needed. Foundational view (Weisberg 1999; Taylor & Greve 2006; Kuhn): only deep local knowledge shows which rules to break and where anomalies are. Burden-of-knowledge work (Jones 2009) points the same way as specialization.
limits: Authors argue the two views are complementary, not exclusive. The tension view dominates management research.
agent_relevance: Maps onto schema operators: anomaly detection from a failing output (foundational) vs analogy to a distant source (tension). Both should exist, gated by signals.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer & Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact, Science 342
finding: From 17.9 million Web of Science papers, journal-pair citations are scored with a z-score against a chance model. The highest-impact papers are mostly conventional in their combinations of prior work but also include a tail of unusual pairings.
numbers: Hit = top 5% of citations at 8 years. 2x2 hit rates per 100 papers: high median conventionality + high tail novelty 9.11; conventional only 5.82; tail novelty only 5.33; neither 2.05; background 5. Shares of papers: 6.7%, 23%, 26%, 44%. P<0.00001. Fewer than 4% of papers have a median z below 0; about 41% have a 10th-percentile z below 0. Same pattern across 243 fields.
quote: Papers of this type were twice as likely to be highly cited works
limits: Journal pairs are a proxy for idea pairs. Citation is the impact measure. Correlational.
agent_relevance: Supports a balanced design: mostly conventional, well-grounded reasoning plus one controlled atypical move. Not a pure far-search strategy.

source: Uzzi et al. (2013) teams and novelty
finding: Team papers include atypical combinations more often than solo papers, with no difference in conventionality.
numbers: High tail novelty in 36.1% (solo), 39.8% (pair), 49.7% (3+ authors) per the text (figure legend gives 36.2 and 39.9); 37.7% higher for teams than solo. K-S tests: solo vs pair P=0.016, pair vs team P=0.001, team vs solo P<0.001. Median conventionality did not differ (P 0.768, 0.417, 0.164).
limits: Correlational; authorship count is not a proxy for idea diversity.
agent_relevance: More independent contributors may add tail novelty, but samples from one model are not independent (G4), so a same-model ensemble will not reproduce this by itself.

source: Wu, Wang & Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology, Nature 566
finding: Across more than 65 million papers, patents and software products (1954-2014), small teams tend to disrupt and large teams tend to develop existing work. Differences grow for higher-impact work. Most of the effect is at the person level as people move between small and large teams.
numbers: 65 million works; period 1954-2014. Abstract page only; full text paywalled and not read.
quote: smaller teams have tended to disrupt science and technology with new ideas and opportunities, whereas larger teams have tended to develop existing ones
limits: Only the abstract was read. The disruption index has known artefact problems (see Holst et al. 2024).
agent_relevance: Small independent probes search deeper into the past; large groups chase recent popular work. Suggests keeping the exploring step lean and not averaged into a crowd.

source: Park, Leahey & Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time, Nature 613
finding: CD index declines over six decades across fields in 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents. The authors link the decline to narrower use of prior knowledge. The page header lists a Matters Arising published 12 August 2026.
numbers: 45 million papers; 3.9 million patents; six datasets (APS, JSTOR, MAG, PatentsView, PubMed, WoS). Abstract page only; full text paywalled.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Reanalysis claims the decline is an artefact (next line).
agent_relevance: Narrowing of which prior work gets used is a plausible failure mode for an agent that retrieves only popular items.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers & Ginis (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science, arXiv 2402.14583
finding: A reanalysis of Park et al. finds the decline in CD index comes from database entries with zero references. A plotting bug hid papers and patents with CD5 = 1 from the histograms. Removing them removes the paper decline and sharply reduces the patent decline. Random citation behaviour in the authors' Monte-Carlo test even reproduces the decline.
numbers: Hidden outliers: 972,161 papers and 142,362 patents with CD5 = 1. In SciSciNet (39,888,199 papers) 97% of CD5=1 papers have zero references; in PatentsView 78% of CD5=1 patents have zero references. Most of those source documents do list references elsewhere.
quote: even random citation behaviour replicates the observed decline in disruptiveness
limits: Preprint (v1, Feb 2024). The original authors may dispute details.
agent_relevance: Warning about measure design: a disruption metric can be driven by data artefacts. Any novelty score we use must be checked against null and random-behaviour baselines.

source: Lin, Evans & Wu (2023) Remote collaboration fuses fewer breakthrough ideas, Nature
finding: Remote teams are consistently less likely to make breakthrough discoveries than on-site teams, across all fields, periods and team sizes. Distributed members mostly share late-stage technical work; conceptual tasks are less shared when knowledge is tacit.
numbers: 20 million research articles; 4 million patent applications; half a century. Abstract only.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Observational.
agent_relevance: Integration of different members' tacit knowledge drives new ideas. Handing off only a codified summary between agent steps may lose what new ideas need.

source: Fleming (2001) Recombinant uncertainty in technological search, Management Science 47
finding: From memory, not read: using new combinations of technology classes lowers the average usefulness of an invention and raises its variance, so both the best and the worst results become more likely. Familiar components and combinations raise the mean.
numbers: Not verified this session. Publisher returned a login page.
limits: Not opened. Citation measure of usefulness.
agent_relevance: Far search is a high-variance strategy: pair it with a cheap code check to cut the bad tail.

source: Singh & Fleming (2010) Lone inventors as sources of breakthroughs: myth or reality? Management Science 56
finding: From memory, not read: patent data show team invention lowers the chance of very poor outcomes and raises the chance of breakthroughs relative to lone inventors. Kaplan and Vakili cite it for the link of novelty to value.
numbers: Not verified this session. Paywalled.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Weak. Background only.

source: Funk & Owen-Smith (2017) A dynamic network measure of technological change, Management Science 63
finding: From memory, not read: defines the consolidation-destabilization (CD) index. A patent is destabilizing if later patents cite it but not the work it cites, consolidating if later patents cite both. The index runs from -1 to +1. Park et al. 2023 use a version of it.
numbers: Not verified this session. Paywalled.
limits: Not opened. Sensitive to zero-reference entries (see Holst et al.) and citation window length.
agent_relevance: Computational definition of a break from the past; could be adapted to an idea graph to check whether a new answer supersedes earlier ones.

source: Trajtenberg, Henderson & Jaffe (1997) University versus corporate patents: a window on the basicness of invention
finding: Seen only as a citation in the Kaplan-Vakili text: originality (synthesis of divergent ideas) goes with high citation counts. Its originality index is the basis of the diversity measure.
numbers: Not verified. Quote carried in Kaplan-Vakili: synthesis of divergent ideas is characteristic of research that is highly original.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background for the originality index.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers, arXiv 2409.04109
finding: Blind expert review of research ideas from three conditions. LLM ideas were scored as more novel than human experts' ideas, with feasibility slightly worse. AI ideas with human rerank scored highest on novelty.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition (human, AI, AI + human rerank); 79 reviewers; 298 reviews; 49 idea writers; 7 NLP topics. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (sd 1.76), AI+rerank 5.81 (sd 1.66); p<0.01 in Test 1 (Welch t-test, Bonferroni, each review independent). Excitement also higher for AI (p<0.05). Agent used Claude-3.5-Sonnet.
quote: LLM-generated ideas are judged as more novel (p < 0.05) than human expert ideas
limits: Ideas, not executed results. Reviewer agreement only 56.1% (NeurIPS 2021: 66.0%; ICLR 2024: 71.9%). Topics restricted to prompting-style NLP research.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty is easy to get from an LLM; it is not evidence of real breakthroughs. See the execution follow-up.

source: Si et al. (2024) limits of LLM ideation and LLM judges
finding: LLM idea generators run out of distinct ideas, and LLM judges do not agree with expert reviewers on ideas.
numbers: Of 4,000 generated seed ideas only 200 were non-duplicates (cosine similarity 0.8 threshold). Claude-3.5 ranker 71.4% accuracy on ICLR accept vs reject (GPT-4o 61.1%, Claude-3-Opus 63.5%). On the idea set, human reviewers agree 56.1%; LLM evaluators 43.3-53.3% (GPT-4o direct 50.0, pairwise 45.0; Claude-3.5 direct 51.7, pairwise 53.3; AI Scientist reviewer 43.3).
limits: Balanced top/bottom 25% task. One study, one domain.
agent_relevance: Supports G5 and G8: do not let a model be the selector of ideas. Over-generating does not help once ideas repeat.

source: Si, Hashimoto & Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap, arXiv 2506.20803
finding: 43 experts executed randomly assigned ideas (human or LLM). LLM ideas had looked better before execution, but after real execution their scores fell far more than human ideas' scores, and the ranking flipped on most metrics.
numbers: N=43 projects (19 human, 24 AI); each over 100 hours of work. Ideation scores human vs AI: novelty 4.91 vs 5.78, excitement 4.40 vs 5.65, effectiveness 4.83 vs 6.00, overall 4.60 vs 5.38. After execution: novelty 4.90 vs 4.73, excitement 4.48 vs 3.90, effectiveness 4.78 vs 4.13, overall 3.97 vs 3.41. Gap for human ideas: -0.01, +0.08, -0.05, -0.63. For AI ideas: -1.05, -1.76, -1.88, -1.98 (AI gaps worse on all four, FDR p 0.025 to 0.001). Direct execution-score differences not significant at idea level (N=43).
quote: the scores of the LLM-generated ideas decrease significantly more than expert-written ideas on all evaluation metrics
limits: Small sample. Ideas were scoped for feasibility. Reviewers saw only 4-page papers.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G8: an idea that looks novel to a judge is not a validated breakthrough. Judge by running the idea.

source: Gupta & Pruthi (2025) All that glitters is not novel: plagiarism in AI-generated research, arXiv 2502.16487
finding: Experts searching for overlap found a quarter of LLM research proposals were paraphrased or heavily borrowed from existing papers. Automated plagiarism checkers missed this.
numbers: 13 experts; 50 LLM-generated research documents; 24.0% had verified plagiarism (one-to-one method mapping or major borrowing), confirmed with source-paper authors; the other 76% showed varying similarity, few fully novel.
limits: Small sample; one generation system family. The expert process was designed to look for plagiarism.
agent_relevance: Judged novelty can come from hidden copying. A novelty check by retrieval against prior work (done in code) is needed.

source: Wang, Downey, Ji & Hope (2024) SciMON: scientific inspiration machines optimized for novelty, arXiv 2305.14259
finding: An LLM system retrieves inspirations from past papers and repeatedly compares its idea with related work to push novelty up. The loop raises novelty but technical depth stays low, and ideas tend to combine popular concepts.
numbers: Iterative novelty boosting: 88.9% of updated ideas substantially different from the initial; 55.6% more novel after iteration 1; 57.8% of continued ideas more novel after iteration 2 (70 instances, 5 annotators). GPT-4 with knowledge-graph input had higher technical detail in 48% of comparisons and was less incremental in 45%; against the original paper's idea, the original was judged better in 85% of comparisons.
limits: Small expert panels. Sentence-level ideas from abstracts, not full research programs.
agent_relevance: A code-controlled loop (retrieve related work, check overlap, revise) raises novelty. Without depth it yields superficial recombination of popular concepts, which matches Kaplan-Vakili.

source: Hu, Fu, Wang et al. (2024) Nova: iterative planning and search to enhance novelty and diversity of LLM generated ideas, arXiv 2410.14255
finding: Iterative planning of what knowledge to retrieve increases the number of unique ideas and top-rated ideas versus earlier idea agents.
numbers: 3.4 times more unique novel ideas than without iterative planning; at least 2.5 times more top-rated ideas than Si et al., Baek et al. and AI Scientist in a Swiss Tournament over 170 seed papers.
limits: Ranking done by LLM and automated judges plus limited human assessment; Si et al. show LLM judges are near chance on ideas.
agent_relevance: Retrieval from the literature widens diversity; treat reported gains as unvalidated until ideas are run or executed.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances creativity but reduces the diversity of novel content, arXiv 2312.00506
finding: Writers with generated story ideas wrote stories rated more novel and useful, but the stories were more similar to each other.
numbers: 293 writers, 600 evaluators. Novelty +6.7% (b=0.259, p=0.001; human-only mean 3.85); usefulness +6.4% (b=0.319, p<0.001; mean 5.02). Stories 5.2% (b=4.29) and 5.0% (b=4.11) closer to the AI idea (both p<0.001); similarity to the within-condition average rose (b=0.871, p<0.001 and b=0.718, p=0.003).
limits: Short stories by crowd workers; story creativity is not scientific breakthrough.
agent_relevance: Each sample looks more creative but a population of LLM-aided outputs converges: another reason same-model samples are not independent (G4).

source: Gu & Krenn (2024) Forecasting high-impact research topics via machine learning on evolving knowledge graphs, arXiv 2402.08640
finding: Builds a semantic graph of concepts and a citation graph from 21 million papers. Trained models (neural net, forest, XGBoost, transformer) predict which unseen concept pairs will be studied and become high impact within years.
numbers: 21,165,421 papers; 368,825 concepts; AUC above 0.9 for most tasks (about 0.90-0.96) vs 0.5 for random.
limits: Predicts links that follow network structure; impact measured by citations; AUC does not show ranking of rare breakthroughs.
agent_relevance: A quantitative selector for promising novelty computed from structure, not from a model's opinion.
